verdict.reasoning: Patient reports left arm numbness and tingling for at least two weeks and worsening: "I'd say for at least two weeks and it's kind of gotten worse. Like, you know, I just kind of felt a little bit of tingling and then it's gotten, it's gotten worse since then. Then the numbing kind of started."
Patient specifies tingling/numbness in digits 2–4 on the palmar side: "Okay, so it's my second, third and fourth finger." and "No, it's the, it's this side. So the front side." (palmar side).

She notes shoulder pain with movement: "sometimes I will feel it in my shoulder. Like if I try to, if I try to like, you know, move like in boxing and stuff, I will even like maybe feel a little bit of, a little bit of pain. But I would say if I'm just like resting..." This describes intermittent shoulder pain with movement.
Denies neck pain: Doctor asks, "Any neck pain at all?" Patient responds, "No, not. No neck pain."

Mild weakness in left upper extremity affecting piano playing: Patient says "I play a little bit of a piano and so I just noticed that it's. It's been kind of harder to get the notes." Doctor summarizes "So you would say there's a mild weakness?" and patient answers "Mild, yes."

No dropping of objects: Doctor asks about dropping things and patient replies, "So not so much with the glass but I will say... I can, I can grasp, I can grasp a glass..." indicating she has not been dropping objects.

Normal gait/legs and weakness only in left arm: Doctor asks, "your weakness is only in your left arm, leg, walking and all this. Normal?" Patient replies, "Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Walking is normal. Yeah."

Temporal association with starting boxing: "I've started taking this boxing class. I've been taking boxing class for a few weeks and I feel like maybe it's probably been, I'd say for at least two weeks..." linking symptom onset to boxing.
Massage and warm baths without relief: "I tried massage, I tried some hot baths and that didn't help with this numbness."

Ibuprofen used for right hand knuckle pain, not helping numbness: She says she takes ibuprofen "just because my, my muscles were sore a little bit... I kind of heard like my knuckles on my right hand" and later notes massage/hot baths "didn't help with this numbness." No benefit to numbness from her taken measures is implied; ibuprofen’s use is clearly for the knuckle soreness.

Transient left eye peripheral visual loss about 20 minutes: "like I all of a sudden just couldn't see from the. From my left eye. Like, I lost some, like a little bit of a field of vision... That just lasted maybe for, I don't know, 20, 20 minutes" and confirmed later by doctor asking duration and patient repeating ~20 minutes a few weeks ago.

Occasional headaches with fatigue: "Sometimes I get headaches, but I think they're just tired headaches... I'll go for a workout and then I'll really just exhaust myself. And then I just kind of feel this fatigue..." linking headaches with tiredness/fatigue.
No seizures: Doctor asks about seizures/fits; patient responds, "Oh, no, no, no, no. Nothing like that. No fits. Yeah."
Does not wear glasses or contacts: Doctor asks, "Do you wear glasses at all? Glasses? Contact lenses?" Patient answers, "No, no. So no glasses."

Summary of left upper extremity paresthesia/mild weakness for ~2 weeks and prior transient left eye visual loss: Supported by earlier quotes on 2 weeks of worsening numbness/tingling and the transient left eye visual loss episode lasting ~20 minutes a few weeks earlier.

No past medical history reported: When asked, patient says, "in general, I'm pretty healthy. I mean, I, you know, I work out a lot, and I don't really have any medical problems." No specific chronic conditions are listed.
Uses ibuprofen as needed: "I do take ibuprofen just because my, my muscles were sore a little bit... I've been taking this boxing class... So I've just kind of taken ibuprofen for that."
Takes vitamin D: "Not really. I just take ibuprofen every once in a while I take vitamin D."
Iron supplement with poor adherence: "I like my g. My GP really wants me to take iron supplements, but you know, there are this like huge pill, so I, most of the time I just forget."
Uses melatonin as needed: "But vitamin D, I take. And then sometimes I take melatonin to help me sleep."
Father with hypothyroidism and autoimmune condition: "I know that my dad has. I don't know if it's hypo. I think it's hypothyroidism. And then my, like he's got some autoimmune stuff going on."

Mother with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol: "my mom... she's got diabetes, type 2, she's got hypertension, she's got. Gosh, what is it? Oh, yeah, she's got high cholesterol" (hyperlipidemia).
No family history of neurologic disease: Doctor asks, "Any neurological conditions in the family? Nerve related conditions?" Patient answers, "No."
Participates in boxing: "I've started taking this boxing class. I've been taking boxing class for a few weeks."
Recent heavy alcohol use: "we were like out partying until, you know, late hours, and I just got uncharacteristically drunk for me."
Exercises regularly: "in general, I'm pretty healthy. I mean, I, you know, I work out a lot" and participation in boxing classes supports regular exercise.
Plays the piano: "well I play a little bit of a piano"

Physician explicitly raises concern for MS/demyelinating disease based on these symptoms: "Sometimes, you know, you do get things like ms, multiple sclerosis. So people with multiple sclerosis can have visual problems like what you've experienced and sometimes, you know, the odd numbness, tingling sensations going on." This is consistent with concern for demyelinating disease and ruling out MS.
Urgent neurology referral: "I'm going to do an urgent, very urgent neurology referral."
Brain imaging anticipated: "What they, what that might entail is the brain scan and things like that." This reasonably implies MRI or similar imaging per neurology.

No steroids or new meds until diagnosis: Patient asks about drugs; doctor replies, "No, that's something we can't do. The treatment for it is actually some steroids... But saying that first we need to adopt firm diagnosis." indicating no steroids/new treatment until confirmed diagnosis.

Emergency precautions for new/progressive weakness, especially legs: "While you're waiting... if there's any weakness, you know, if the weakness progresses to your legs... then that would be an A." (emergency).

Emergency precautions for severe headache: Included in same warning: "if there's any weakness... or there's any kind of headaches, vomiting, fits, and your visual symptoms are getting worse... then that would be an A."
Emergency precautions for vomiting: Same sentence: "or there's any kind of headaches, vomiting, fits, and your visual symptoms are getting worse... then that would be an A."
Emergency precautions for fits/seizures: "or there's any kind of headaches, vomiting, fits, and your visual symptoms are getting worse... then that would be an A."
Emergency precautions for worsening visual symptoms: "and your visual symptoms are getting worse and not getting better, then that would be an A."
